extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism; editors/annotators of Victorian essays
extracted.subtask_description: Annotations and explanatory notes to Matthew Arnold's essays (references, glosses, critical asides) intended to guide readers' understanding of literary-historical and aesthetic points. Focuses on descriptive-analytic commentary rather than a prescriptive how-to, but it contains embedded evaluative remarks about poetry and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical 'false notes' in nature-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a crying false note, which carries us at once out of the world of nature-magic, and the breath of the woods, into the world of theatre-magic and the smell of gas and orange-peel." (on the passage rendering Tieck's 'high funguses' as a stagey image)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold's critical point: overly theatrical, sensational, or self-consciously fantastic imagery in nature-poetry is an anti-pattern; it betrays inauthenticity and breaks the reader's immersion in natural 'magic'. The note contrasts 'born lover of nature' tact/delicacy with clumsy stage effects; use this as a warning against exaggerated, theatrical diction in nature description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme as a principal source of modern poetry's 'romantic element'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rhyme,--the most striking characteristic of our modern poetry as distinguished from that of the ancients, and a main source, to our poetry, of its magic and charm, of what we call its _romantic element_--rhyme itself, all the weight of evidence tends to show, comes into our poetry from the Celts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold treats presence/use of rhyme as a defining formal feature that supplies modern (romantic) charm. The note also records an alternate view (J. Schipper) that end-rhyme arose independently and spread via church hymns — useful when assessing origins/justification for formal choices. As an evaluative criterion, degree and use of rhyme contribute to a poem's romantic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Champion adherence to the 'national type' in literature (Herder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Herder: he 'championed adherence to the national type in literature, and helped to found the historical method in literature and science.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit evaluative standard: literary works gain authenticity and value when they accord with or arise from a people's national/linguistic/cultural type. Useful criterion when judging national/folk elements, vernacular modes, or historic fidelity in literary composition and criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek 'sweetness and light' in literary culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation/explanation: Swift's apologue summarized as furnishing mankind with 'the two noblest of things, which are sweetness and light.' (Arnold's 'Sweetness and Light' chapter reference)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold's aesthetic ideal: literature/culture should cultivate both pleasurable style ('sweetness') and intellectual/moral illumination ('light'). Use this dual standard to evaluate prose or poetry for lyrical grace and clarifying, civilizing insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'sentimental excesses' characteristic of Werther-style Romanticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mention: Goethe's _Werther_ 'was a product of the _Sturm und Drang_ movement in German literature, and responsible for its sentimental excesses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an evaluative caution: works that indulge uncontrolled sentiment can be criticized for excess and dangerous imitation. Use restraint and measure of feeling as a criterion when assessing emotional tone and its social effects in fiction and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Criticism of life' as a criterion for literary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Arnold's phrase 'criticism of life' (see _The Study of Poetry_, Note 1) and repeated allusions to criticism engaging with life and ethical dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit rubric: literary criticism should connect texts to lived experience and moral/ethical bearings — not merely formalist or scholastic analysis. Evaluate criticism on whether it meaningfully interprets a work's relation to life, society, and ethical purpose.
